title: Bering's Great Northern Expedition
summary: The Great Northern Expedition (1733-1743) was a Russian effort led by Vitus Bering to find whether Asia and America were joined. In July 1741 his ship St. Peter reached Kayak Island off Alaska, where the naturalist Georg Steller made what many consider the first scientific investigation of northwestern North America. Bering died after the ship wintered on a Commander island on the way home.

uncertainty.note: The National Park Service gives the Great Northern Expedition as 1733-1743; Bering's own voyage to America ran from June 1741 to late 1742. Dates inside the voyage differ between sources (16 vs 17 July sighting, the NPS date being Julian; death 8 vs 19 December 1741).

as_recorded.value: On the 17th of July (Julian calendar), lookouts on St. Peter
on 16 July 1741 sighted Alaska; four days later he landed on Kayak Island

where.modern_name: Kayak Island, Gulf of Alaska, United States (landing site)
where.historical_name: Kayak Island in the Gulf of Alaska, Sugpiaq and Eyak territory (per NPS), not claimed by any European state

waypoints.label: Saint Petersburg: the first detachments left in February 1733.
Okhotsk: preparations were completed by 1740 before the expedition sailed to Kamchatka.
Kayak Island: a watering party, including Steller, went ashore on July 20.
Bering Island (Commander Islands): the crew wintered here and Bering died in December 1741.

importance.justification: Produced the first documented investigation of Alaska by Europeans and extended Russia's knowledge of the North Pacific.

sources.title: Bering Expedition Landing Site National Historic Landmark

reviewer_note: Least sure: exact days. NPS says 17 July (Julian) sighting, Gale says 16 July; Bering's death is 8 December in one Gale entry and 19 December in another on the same page. Survivor counts differ (NPS 46 led by Waxell; Gale 45 of 77), so none is given. Okhotsk year 1740 comes from "by 1740 preparations at Okhotsk were completed". Bering Island and Okhotsk Wikidata points are rounded.

beats.caption: The expedition's first detachments leave Saint Petersburg and cross Siberia toward Okhotsk.
On July 20, 1741 a watering party goes ashore on Kayak Island, where Steller finds signs of recent human activity.
The voyage report and Steller's journal form the first documented investigation of Alaska, though Bering died on the way home.
